segments.title: The Fog and What It Hides: Opening the World of Bleak House

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, unhurried conversation about one of the great novels in the English language.
Bleak House is the novel in which Dickens perfected his art — the fog, the labyrinthine lawsuit, the vast cast of characters all enmeshed in one another's fates.
Each episode we take a set of passages and ask: what is Dickens actually doing here, and why does it still matter?
Today we're beginning at the beginning — the fog, and what it conceals.
Joining me are three guests whose company I can promise you will make this novel feel both utterly familiar and completely new.

Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads fiction the way a watchmaker reads a movement — she sees every gear and spring, and she can tell you why the whole thing sings.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes the novel's genius lies in its moral imagination — in the individual souls caught in Dickens's great machine.
And Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more classic novels for audio than perhaps any living person — he hears Dickens the way Dickens heard himself, as performance, as voice, as rhythm.
Let us start where Dickens starts: with the fog, and with Chancery, and with the question of what the law does to the people trapped inside it.
What strikes me every time I return to this novel is how early Dickens establishes what I'd call the structural joke at its heart.
The suit of Jarndyce and Jarndyce is a machine that appears to process justice but actually consumes everything it touches.
And then he gives us Gridley — the man from Shropshire — who embodies that consumption in human form.
Dickens writes this as though the Chancery has literally worn the man's skin away.
Gridley says — and this is the line that stops me every time —
"I have been dragged for five and twenty years over burning iron, and I have lost the habit of treading upon velvet."
That opposition — burning iron, velvet — does so much work in so few words.
It's not merely about rudeness or poverty — it's about a man whose sensory experience of life has been permanently altered by the law.
Eleanor is right to isolate that image, and I think it points to something rather more specific than structural satire.
What Dickens understands — and what makes him morally serious rather than merely polemical — is that the law destroys character.
Not just finances, not just time — character itself.
Mr. Jarndyce explains the suit to Esther with what I can only call magnificent exasperation.
He describes how equity sends questions to law, and law sends them back — endlessly, pointlessly — and then arrives at this:
"And thus, through years and years, and lives and lives, everything goes on, constantly beginning over and over again, and nothing ever ends."
The repetition there — years and years, lives and lives — is not rhetorical decoration.
It is the formal enactment of the very futility he is describing.
Dickens is not simply an entertainer with a grievance — he is a moralist who has found the perfect dramatic form for his indignation.
Edmund, I'd agree entirely — and I'd add that when you read that passage aloud, the prose itself starts to behave like the Chancery suit.
It loops, it cross-references, it refers you back to what you've already heard — you almost lose the thread, which is precisely the point.
Dickens was a performer himself — he knew that the sentence had to be experienced in time, not just read on the page.
Now — speaking of rooms that tell us exactly who their occupant is — I want to bring in Skimpole, because he is the comic counterpoint to all this suffering.
We visit his lodgings, and Esther describes them in a sentence I've always loved for its sheer audacity.

"It was dingy enough and not at all clean, but furnished with an odd kind of shabby luxury, with a large footstool, a sofa, and plenty of cushions, an easy-chair, and plenty of pillows, a piano, books, drawing materials, music, newspapers, and a few sketches and pictures."
And then — a broken pane of glass papered over, but a little plate of hothouse nectarines on the table.
That is Skimpole in one detail: the window broken, the nectarines fresh.
He never repairs anything, but he always has fruit.
That's a perfect reading — and what makes it formally interesting is that Esther's narration doesn't editorialize.
She simply lists — the footstool, the sofa, the cushions, the pillows — and the accumulation does all the moral work.
The list itself is a kind of Chancery, isn't it — endless, self-replicating, arriving nowhere conclusive.
Dickens has found a prose style that mirrors his subject — and he uses it for comedy and tragedy with equal precision.
I'd only note that Skimpole's irresponsibility is not merely comic — it has victims.
The nectarines are purchased with other people's money, and Dickens never lets us quite forget that.
There is something of the Chancery in Skimpole too — a system that produces nothing and consumes everything around it.
Oliver's detail about the nectarines is delightful — but Dickens intends the delight to curdle slightly, if one is paying attention.
Edmund, you are absolutely right, and I speak as someone who finds Skimpole irresistible and genuinely monstrous in roughly equal measure.
But before we leave the question of what the law does to the poor — there's a passage I keep returning to about Jo.
The omniscient narrator addresses Jo directly — steps outside the story to speak to him.
And he describes Jo as — despite everything the law says about him —
"not quite in outer darkness."
And then he gives us what Jo has said — this illiterate boy's testimony:
"He wos wery good to me, he wos!"
The misspelling is the whole point — the novel refuses to correct Jo's voice into respectability.
That is where Dickens's moral imagination lives — not in the courts, but in eight words of imperfect gratitude.
The fog, the lawsuit, the nectarines, the boy in the street — all part of the same vast design.
In a moment, we'll look more closely at how Dickens builds atmosphere into something that feels almost like fate.
Stay with us.

segments.title: The Architecture of Corruption: Narrative Technique and the Court of Chancery

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel apart — sentence by sentence, image by image — to find out how it works and why it endures.
I'm your host, and today we're asking a question that sits at the very heart of this novel: how does Dickens build his world?
Not merely what it contains — the fog, the court, the secrets — but the extraordinary technical machinery that makes it all feel inevitable.
Joining me today are three guests who between them cover every dimension of how a novel like this gets made and received.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose great passion is the architecture of literary effects — the way a single structural choice can illuminate an entire book.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads Dickens as a moralist first and a social satirist second — and makes a compelling case for that reading every time.
And Oliver Trevelyan is the actor and writer who has recorded more classic novel audiobooks than perhaps any living person — he comes to every text as a performer, hearing what others merely read.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — and with the very first thing Dickens gives us in this novel.
The opening of Bleak House is one of the most audacious gambits in the history of the English novel.
Dickens gives us no character, no scene, no dialogue — just a condition.
He simply announces the state of the world, and the word he uses is the most important single word in the book.
"Fog everywhere."
Two words, and the entire moral atmosphere of the novel is already in place.
Then Dickens expands it, almost obsessively — he won't let the fog go.
"Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city."
Notice the parenthesis — "and dirty" — dropped in with such casual contempt, as though the narrator can barely suppress a private joke at London's expense.
When I first recorded that passage, I had to stop after the opening sentence.
Because Dickens has written it for the voice, not the eye.
The repetition of "fog" — seven, eight, nine times — is not a rhetorical flourish; it's a drumbeat.
It's relentless, almost hypnotic, and by the time you reach the shivering apprentice boy on deck, you feel as trapped as he is.
What's remarkable to me is how Dickens moves from the vast — the Essex marshes, the Kentish heights — down to the extraordinarily intimate.
"Fog cruelly pinching the toes and fingers of his shivering little 'prentice boy on deck."
That word "cruelly" is doing such extraordinary work — the fog has become an agent, a persecutor.
I want to gently resist the reading of fog purely as political metaphor — Chancery as fog, capitalism as fog, and so forth.
What Dickens is doing here is something more ancient and more human — he is establishing a world in which suffering is the common lot.
The Greenwich pensioners wheezing by their firesides and the apprentice boy shivering on deck are not ciphers for a social system — they are individual human beings being made miserable.
That, I would argue, is the moral atmosphere Eleanor rightly identifies — not a programme, but a vision of human vulnerability.
Edmund, I think we're closer than we appear — and I'll show you why through a very different passage.
In chapter eleven, Dickens gives us the dead body of Nemo — the unknown man, the man without a name.
And the narrator performs something astonishing: he imagines the dead man's mother looking at her infant son and then asks —
"Oh, if in brighter days the now-extinguished fire within him ever burned for one woman who held him in her heart, where is she, while these ashes are above the ground!"
"These ashes" — a dead man, referred to as ashes while his body is still above ground.
The narrator is performing grief — or rather, performing the grief that no living person has come to perform.
That is both a moral gesture, Edmund, and a structural one — the novel itself mourns what society has left unmourned.
That is beautifully put, and I concede the point — with one qualification.
The narrator's grief is genuine and particularised — it is for this man, not for a class or an abstraction.
Dr. Johnson observed that general expressions of human misery carry no weight unless the reader can feel the particular case.
Dickens passes that test magnificently here — "the now-extinguished fire within him" is about one human soul.
And then — almost in the same breath — Dickens gives us Jo.
Jo, the crossing-sweeper — the character most utterly bereft in the novel — comes to this same wretched burial ground.
And what does he do? He sweeps it.
"It then, with an old broom it carries, softly sweeps the step and makes the archway clean."
"It" — not "he." Dickens uses "it" for Jo throughout this passage.
A child so dehumanised by his condition that even the narrator's pronoun refuses him full humanity — and yet the act he performs is one of pure, wordless devotion.
I find that almost unbearable to read aloud.
Let's stay with the question of narrative technique for a moment — and move from the omniscient narrator to the other voice in this novel: Esther Summerson.
Eleanor, you've been thinking about what happens when Dickens hands the narration over to Esther — a narrator who, as you've pointed out, is notably reluctant to claim authority.
Esther is the most technically interesting narrator in Victorian fiction, and she is also the most deceptive — deceptive in the most generous sense.
She claims she doesn't know things, that she can barely interpret what she sees — and then reveals, through the very structure of her sentences, that she knows everything.
There's a moment in chapter six where she describes a glance from Mr. Jarndyce — just a glance — and unpacks it with extraordinary precision.
"I felt as if in that moment he confided to me — and knew that he confided to me and that I received the confidence — his hope that Ada and Richard might one day enter on a dearer relationship."
The triple clause — confided, knew that he confided, and that she received the confidence — is a phenomenology of a single wordless exchange.
Esther doesn't just notice the communication — she models how mutual understanding works between two people who trust each other implicitly.
And this is where I part company with those who find Esther cloying or self-deprecating to the point of dishonesty.
That passage Eleanor has just read is a portrait of a character of genuine moral intelligence — someone who understands not just what was communicated but how and why it was communicated.
Esther is good in the way that characters in novels are rarely permitted to be good — specifically, lucidly, without sentimentality.
The challenge of reading Esther aloud is precisely that — you must never let her seem to know too much, even as she knows everything.
The voice has to be guileless and alert simultaneously — it's one of the hardest tonal balances in English prose narrative.
Eleanor, you've also been looking at how the omniscient narrator handles spaces — particularly abandoned spaces — as the novel moves toward its darker second half.
There's a passage in chapter fifty-eight that I consider one of the most formally perfect pieces of Gothic prose Dickens ever wrote.
Lady Dedlock has fled; her rooms stand empty.
And the narrator — suddenly, startlingly — turns to address the reader directly before arriving at the central image.
"Dark and cold as the wintry day is, it is darker and colder in these deserted chambers than in many a hut that will barely exclude the weather."
The comparison is devastating — a great house, cold beyond the cold of any hovel.
And then the sentence that makes it unbearable: "there is a heavy cloud upon the rooms which no light will dispel."
We've come all the way from the fog of chapter one to this — a cloud that is now interior, moral, permanent.
That architectural movement — fog to cloud, exterior to interior — is the shape of the entire novel.
Dickens begins by placing the fog everywhere outside, and ends by placing it inside the grandest house in England.
I want to pause on the sentence Eleanor quoted — "as all partings foreshadow the great final one."
That is not a political observation. That is a theological one — or at least a metaphysical one.
Dickens is writing about death — not about class, but about the universal diminishment that awaits every human being, in every room.
Edmund is right — and that's precisely what makes Tulkinghorn so terrifying a counterweight to all of this.
Because Tulkinghorn is not interested in death, metaphysics, or suffering — he is interested only in managed revelation.
He says to Lady Dedlock, with this horrible jog-trot reasonableness —
"If I inflicted this shock upon him to-morrow morning, how could the immediate change in him be accounted for? What could have caused it?"
He's not asking out of compassion for Sir Leicester — he's asking because a visible shock is a loose end, and Tulkinghorn cannot abide loose ends.
The fog, in his hands, is not an atmosphere to be mourned — it is a management tool.
There is something deeply unsettling about that — the corruption of the institutional world manifesting not in grand villainy but in that jog-trot reasonableness Eleanor names.
We'll be returning to Tulkinghorn and to the question of power in this novel in our next segment.
But what today's discussion has already made clear is that the architecture of Bleak House — its fog, its dual narration, its empty rooms — is not decoration.
It is the argument of the novel, made visible — and audible.

segments.title: Richard's Spiral: Ambition, Hope, and Disillusionment

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel apart, passage by passage, to see how it works and why it endures.
Today's segment is about Richard Carstone — perhaps the novel's most heartbreaking portrait of a young man undone not by villainy but by hope.
With me are three guests who know this novel with unusual intimacy.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative-writing teacher who reads Dickens above all as a craftsman — alert to every structural choice, every image that carries more than its apparent weight.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who has spent a lifetime arguing that what makes a great novel great is its moral imagination — its picture of human character tested by circumstance.
And Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more classic-novel audiobooks than perhaps any other living actor — he hears the prose as performance, and no one alive is better company inside a Dickens paragraph.
We begin with Mr. Jarndyce's counsel to Richard and Ada — a moment of extraordinary tenderness that also, if you read it carefully, contains the seed of everything that follows.
What strikes me every time I return to this chapter is how Jarndyce frames his counsel as a deliberate act of restraint.
He announces, almost formally, what he will not say — the warnings about inconstancy, the chain of flowers becoming a chain of lead — and then declines to say it.
But of course he has said it, in the very act of naming what he is withholding.
That is a very sophisticated piece of narrative architecture — the warning delivered under a veil of non-warning.
And then he offers what is genuinely generous — the promise that if they do change, there will be no shame in it.
He says, and this is the passage I keep coming back to:

"if you DO change — if you DO come to find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and woman than you were as boy and girl — don't be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be nothing monstrous or uncommon in it."
That word 'monstrous' is doing tremendous work — it pre-emptively redeems the very change he most fears.
One cannot read Jarndyce's speech without feeling the weight of its moral seriousness.
He is not merely offering kindness — he is modelling what genuine guardianship looks like: power utterly renounced.
He says so explicitly: 'I have no power over you whatever.'
That is a man of genuine virtue speaking — not a man performing virtue for approval.
And then, when he turns to counsel Richard directly, we hear perhaps the finest single passage of practical moral wisdom in the entire novel.
'Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner.'
The allusion to the waggoner who prayed to Hercules without first putting his own shoulder to the wheel is exactly right — elegant, economical, unshowy.
The tragedy, of course, is that Richard hears these words and almost immediately begins to act in precise contradiction of them.
I've read that speech aloud more times than I can count, and it never loses its peculiar doubleness.
Because Dickens gives Jarndyce this wonderful parenthetical — 'your manhood will excuse me, Rick!' — right in the middle of the most serious passage.
It's a tiny comic breath, a little release of pressure — and it makes the tenderness on either side of it feel more real, not less.
But what I most want to linger on is that final injunction about effort — because Dickens doesn't soften it.

'If you entertain the supposition that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts, leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here.'
The rhythmic repetition — 'ever was or could be, ever will or can be' — that's not rhetoric for rhetoric's sake.
It's the sound of a man trying to drive something home — knowing, perhaps, that it won't go in.
And what follows Jarndyce's counsel is one of the most quietly devastating images in the whole novel.
Esther watches Ada and Richard walk away through a sunlit room — and then she tells us what she saw.
This is the passage I would choose if I were asked to teach how atmosphere becomes prophecy in a single paragraph.
Esther doesn't editorialize — she simply describes what she sees and what the light does.

'So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness.'
'So they passed away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over.'
The architecture is almost musical — a crescendo of hope followed by an immediate, quiet collapse.
And crucially, the sun clouds over not when anything bad happens — but simply when they leave the room.
Their departure is itself the shadow — which is a genuinely frightening thing for a narrator to imply.
I take the point about atmosphere — but I want to insist on the human fact at the centre of that image.
Esther tells us that Richard walks with his head bent, talking to Ada very earnestly, and that Ada looks up at him and seems to see nothing else.
That is a portrait of absolute mutual absorption — two young people entirely inside their own world.
It is beautiful, and it is also, in retrospect, the precise shape of their vulnerability — they cannot yet see what Jarndyce sees.
And we have confirmation of that troubled vision just pages later, when Esther notes something she has never observed in Jarndyce before.
'This was the first time I ever saw him follow Ada with his eyes with something of a shadow on their benevolent expression.'
A shadow on benevolent eyes — it is the same shadow that fell over the room when Ada and Richard departed.
Dickens is binding these images together with a precision that repays the closest attention.
Edmund has put his finger on something I think is easily missed — the way Esther herself is implicated in that observation.
She notices the shadow — and Jarndyce then turns a silent look of confidence toward her.
He is not merely worried — he is transferring something of his worry to someone he trusts.
And Esther understands this completely, even as she cannot yet name what it is that troubles him.
Which brings us to the question of how quickly Richard's 'tremendous ardour' for the law curdles into something else entirely.
Yes — and the passage where Richard explains his reasons for joining Kenge's office is rather extraordinary for the casual self-revelation it contains.
It is barely disguised, is it — the way the obsession surfaces even as he tries to frame it as professional diligence.
He says he wants to study law — but then immediately qualifies it with this tell-tale pause:
'I should have my eye on the — hum! — the forbidden ground — and should be able to study it, and master it.'
That 'hum!' — that tiny hesitation — is one of Dickens's most accomplished comic strokes.

Richard has been told explicitly that the Chancery suit is off-limits, and here he is literally stumbling over the prohibition in mid-sentence — and then naming it 'forbidden ground' as if he's perfectly aware of the irony.
The law, for Richard, was never really the law — it was always just a door labelled 'Jarndyce and Jarndyce.'
I have to say, that 'hum!' is one of the great pleasures of recording Dickens — you feel the character seizing up in real time.
And then 'peg away at Blackstone and all those fellows with the most tremendous ardour' — the ardour is already comic, already hollow.
Dickens is showing us, through rhythm alone, that Richard believes his own story — and that the story is wrong.
The gap between what he says and what he means is precisely the size of the disaster ahead.
I want to resist the temptation to read this purely as a social critique of Chancery's corrupting influence — though that is certainly present.
What Dickens gives us is also a study in the particular weakness of a generous temperament without ballast.
Richard is not wicked — he is sanguine to the point of self-destruction.
Esther uses that word — 'my poor, dear, sanguine Richard' — and it is the most sorrowful epithet in the novel because it names his virtue as his ruin.
His fault is not cynicism or greed — it is an incapacity to doubt his own brightest expectations.
And by the time we reach chapter twenty-three, the shape of the catastrophe is fully visible — even if Richard cannot see it.
Esther tells us he has 'got at the core of that mystery' — his phrase — and yet what he has found at the core is only deeper delusion.
And then she gives us the image that, for me, crystallises the entire arc.

'Every one of them sunk him deeper in the infatuation... what a fatal link was riveting between his fresh youth and her faded age, between his free hopes and her caged birds, and her hungry garret, and her wandering mind.'
The pairing of his 'free hopes' with her 'caged birds' — that is an image of such structural precision it takes your breath away.
Because freedom and imprisonment are the same condition here — they just belong to different stages of the same journey.
Miss Flite is one of the great comic grotesques in all of Dickens — and yet Dickens never lets us forget what she actually is.
She is Richard's future — his precise, literal future — walking around in a bonnet and talking about the judgment.
And what is unbearable — properly unbearable — is that he laughs at her.
Esther says so: 'while he laughed at her, he pitied her from his heart.'
He cannot see the mirror Dickens has placed directly in front of him.
And that blindness — that specifically young, specifically hopeful blindness — is what makes Richard's story tragic rather than merely cautionary.
Richard Carstone — seen as the brightest hope in the novel's opening pages, and already carrying his destruction within him by the time we have truly come to love him.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Sir Edmund Leigh, and Oliver Trevelyan for a conversation of unusual depth and warmth.
We'll continue unpacking Bleak House in our next segment — and the novel, as ever, has more to give.

segments.title: The Weight of Secrets: Lady Dedlock's Hidden Past and Its Unraveling

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the show where we take Dickens's great fog-bound masterpiece apart, passage by passage, to see how it works and why it endures.
Today we're entering the novel's dark interior — the gravitational pull at Bleak House's centre: Lady Dedlock's secret.
Three voices join me for this conversation.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens with the eye of a fellow craftsman — always asking how the effect is made.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who insists, with great conviction and considerable charm, that the novel's moral imagination matters far more than its social argument.
And Oliver Trevelyan has read more Dickens aloud than almost anyone alive — he hears the prose the way a musician hears a score.

We begin with Mr. Jarndyce's extraordinary revelation to Esther in Chapter Seventeen — the letter from the mysterious lady, the orphan girl, and the web of secrecy that has shaped Esther's entire life.
What strikes me first about this scene is the architecture of disclosure — the way Dickens layers the revelation through Jarndyce's narration rather than giving it to us directly.
We're hearing a letter described, not read. We're at two removes from the original voice.
And Dickens uses that distance brilliantly — it creates a sense of something hidden even in the act of telling.
Listen to how Jarndyce characterises the letter itself — before we even hear its contents.
"It was written to me, perhaps because it was the writer's idiosyncrasy to put that trust in me, perhaps because it was mine to justify it."
That doubling — the writer's nature, and Jarndyce's own fitness to receive such a trust — is quietly devastating.
It tells us everything about John Jarndyce's character without a single explicit statement of virtue.
I think you're quite right about Jarndyce, and it's worth dwelling on that for a moment.
What we are witnessing here is not merely narrative architecture, as you put it, but a portrait of genuine moral seriousness in a man.
Jarndyce receives a letter from a woman steeped in shame and guilt, and his response is not judgment — it is compassion.
Dickens is careful to note the nature of the writer's distress — and here the passage on religion is quite extraordinary.
"The distorted religion which clouded her mind with impressions of the need there was for the child to expiate an offence of which she was quite innocent."
That word — distorted — is doing tremendous moral work.
Dickens is not condemning religion — he is condemning a religion warped by guilt into cruelty visited upon a blameless child.
It is a very precise moral distinction, and Dickens makes it without flinching.
Edmund's point about Jarndyce's compassion is well taken — but I want to go back to the letter itself for a moment, because as a performer this passage absolutely electrifies me.
The letter is described as written with — and this is Dickens's precise phrase — "a stern passion and power that rendered it unlike all other letters I have ever read."
Stern passion — that pairing is extraordinary on the tongue.
It tells you everything about Lady Dedlock before she ever appears in this context — a woman whose emotions are iron-caged, volcanic underneath.
And then the content — an orphan girl, friendless, nameless, unknown. Dickens stacks those three words and each one lands harder than the last.
When you read that aloud, the rhythm itself is the argument — there is nowhere left for the child to exist.
Oliver, that's exactly it — the tricolon is doing something that no amount of explanation could do.
But I want to move to what I think is the most chilling moment in these chapters — the final revelation of what the mysterious lady would and would not disclose.
Jarndyce reports what Mr. Kenge learned — and this is the passage that stopped me cold on first reading.

"That she was, if there were any ties of blood in such a case, the child's aunt. That more than this she would never — and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution — for any human consideration disclose."
The qualification — "if there were any ties of blood in such a case" — is doing enormous legal and emotional work simultaneously.
She will admit just enough to secure Esther's future — and not one syllable more.
The architecture of concealment is as precise as a legal document — and as devastating as a confession.
One must also note what Dickens records about the assumed name.
"The lady said, of her own accord and not of his seeking, that her name was an assumed one."
Of her own accord — she volunteers this intelligence without pressure.
It suggests a conscience still capable of demanding some partial honesty, even as the larger secret is hermetically sealed.
This is a woman of great moral complexity — she is not simply a villain concealing wickedness, but a soul conducting a terrible negotiation with her own guilt.
That negotiation with guilt — Edmund, I think you've named the pulse of the whole subplot.
And Dickens then performs a kind of miracle in Chapter Eighteen, when Esther actually encounters Lady Dedlock for the first time — without knowing who she is.
The reader knows more than Esther does. The dramatic irony is almost unbearable — and then Dickens compounds it with something even stranger.
Esther feels something — something she cannot name or explain, reaching back into her earliest childhood.

"And, very strangely, there was something quickened within me, associated with the lonely days at my godmother's; yes, away even to the days when I had stood on tiptoe to dress myself at my little glass after dressing my doll."
Standing on tiptoe to dress herself at her little glass after dressing her doll — the specific, achingly particular detail of a lonely child's morning ritual.
And this is all conjured by a fashionable woman she has never, she is absolutely certain, seen before in her life.
What Dickens is dramatising there is something almost pre-rational — a cellular memory, a recognition below the threshold of conscious thought.
And he's careful to have Esther herself interrogate the feeling — she considers whether Lady Dedlock resembles her godmother, and rejects it.
The expression is entirely different, she says — Lady Dedlock's face lacks the severity that had, as Dickens writes, "worn into my godmother's face, like weather into rocks."
That simile — weather into rocks — is Dickens at his most compressed and his most Gothic.
But then Esther arrives at the passage that I think is the emotional core of these two chapters.

"And yet I — I, little Esther Summerson, the child who lived a life apart and on whose birthday there was no rejoicing — seemed to arise before my own eyes, evoked out of the past by some power in this fashionable lady."
"Little Esther Summerson" — she names herself in the third person, as though she is watching herself be conjured.
The self becomes an object of perception — and the agent of that conjuring is her own mother, whom she doesn't yet know.
Eleanor has identified what I would call the novel's deepest emotional gamble, and I think it succeeds brilliantly.
Dickens is asking us to believe that the bond between mother and child operates beneath knowledge, beneath memory, beneath the reach of reason.
It is a profoundly conservative instinct, in the deepest sense of that word — the claim that certain human connections are not made but discovered.
The birthday with no rejoicing — that detail from the passage stops me every time.
It is the one day in a year when a child's existence is supposed to be celebrated — and for Esther, it was the day of her shame.
And yet here, this fashionable woman has unknowingly called her back into being — given her, in some private and unspeakable way, the recognition she was always denied.
I think what undoes me, every time I read or perform this passage, is that tiny doubled pronoun at the start — "And yet I — I."
Two syllables, one repetition — and suddenly Esther's composure, that tremendous narrative composure she maintains across hundreds of pages, cracks open for just a moment.
When you perform it, you have to resist the temptation to make too much of it — the genius is that Dickens has already made everything of it.
Your job as a reader is simply to let the silence after that second "I" do its work.
And perhaps that's where we leave this thread — in that silence after the second "I," where Esther stands at the threshold of a truth she cannot yet see.

We've traced the secret from its concealed origin in Jarndyce's letter to its uncanny surfacing in Esther's nervous system — and the novel hasn't yet given either of them the words for what they feel.
That gap between felt knowledge and spoken knowledge is, as Edmund, Eleanor, and Oliver have shown us, where Dickens does some of his most extraordinary work.
Coming up: we turn to the fog of Chancery itself — the lawsuit that devours lives, and the terrible comedy Dickens makes of institutional cruelty.

segments.title: Jo's Testimony: Dickens and the Voiceless in a Broken System

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast where we take Dickens's great novel one passage at a time.
Today's segment asks a question that sits at the moral heart of the novel: what does Dickens do with the people the system cannot see?
We have three brilliant readers with us, and I want to introduce them properly.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — she sees every gear.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who insists, with a certain magnificent stubbornness, that great fiction is finally about individual moral character.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has read more Dickens aloud than almost any living person — brings us the sound of the prose, the timing, the theatricality.
We begin with the children — and with the extraordinary range of ways Dickens places a child before us.
What strikes me immediately, moving through these passages, is how Dickens controls the temperature of his children.
The Pardiggle boys and Tom Neckett exist in the same novel, breathe the same foggy London air — and yet Dickens pitches them in completely different emotional registers.
The Pardiggle children are comic — grotesquely, brilliantly comic.
Esther's narration sets up the observation with devastating precision.
"We had never seen such dissatisfied children. It was not merely that they were weazened and shrivelled — though they were certainly that too — but they looked absolutely ferocious with discontent."
That word 'ferocious' — applied to small, malnourished children in a drawing room — is a tiny structural explosion.
Esther is using comic exaggeration to indict Mrs. Pardiggle, but she never quite winks at us — the indictment lands through the image itself.
Eleanor, yes — and performing that passage you feel the comedy running on a very short leash above something quite cruel.
Dickens gives Egbert — this tiny, starved child — the most magnificent moment of the sequence.
Esther says, and I love this — she says she could really have supposed him to be one of the most baleful members of the Tockahoopo Indians, given the savage frown he directed at her.
As a performer you think: that is a six-year-old's revenge fantasy written by a man who was himself a hungry child pressed into labour.
The comedy is entirely on the children's side.
Mrs. Pardiggle is the butt — not these ferocious, weazened, entirely reasonable little insurgents.
I'll grant the comedy gladly — Dickens's comic timing in that passage is impeccable.
But what interests me morally is the contrast with young Tom Neckett — and that contrast is not comic at all.
Dickens places Esther before a door, applies a key, and reveals something that has the quality of a moral judgement rendered in a single image.
"In a poor room with a sloping ceiling and containing very little furniture was a mite of a boy, some five or six years old, nursing and hushing a heavy child of eighteen months."
There is no commentary needed.
The sloping ceiling pressing down, the cold, the shrunken figures — Dickens trusts the scene entirely.
That boy's act of nursing is, in its small way, a form of heroism — and it shames every organised institution in the novel.
Edmund, that's exactly right, and what's technically so impressive is the point-of-view choice.
Esther is the witness — the key turns and the reader sees through her eyes.
The Pardiggle children are given to us with Esther's quiet irony; Tom is given with Esther's utter silence about her own reaction.
She simply describes what she sees — noses red and pinched, small figures shrunken — and then stops.
The reader's distress is not prompted — it is produced, almost physiologically, by the accumulation of observed detail.
Now — from the child who nurses in silence, to the child who cannot even explain himself when he is called to speak.
Jo, the crossing-sweeper, who looks in through the cemetery gate — and who appears, briefly, as a name in the court testimony of Mrs. Piper.
The cemetery passage is twelve words long — give or take — and it is one of the most devastating things in the novel.
Dickens writes, simply:

"With the night comes a slouching figure through the tunnel-court to the outside of the iron gate. It holds the gate with its hands and looks in between the bars, stands looking in for a little while."
'It.' Not 'he.' 'It.'
That pronoun carries the entire argument of the novel in two letters.
Jo has been so thoroughly deprived of status, of name, of witness — the narrative itself initially refuses him personhood.
And then he stands at the bars and looks in — and grief does the rest.
Oliver has put his finger on something I find genuinely moving, though I would press it in a slightly different direction.
The pronoun 'it' is, I think, less a political statement than a grammatical enactment of invisibility.
Dickens is not editorialising — he is showing us how the world sees Jo before it has learned, as we are about to learn, to see him at all.
That is the novel's moral project — not a reform pamphlet, but a reorientation of vision.
And Mrs. Piper's testimony is the counter-example — she talks at great length and sees absolutely nothing.
Mrs. Piper — now there is a virtuoso comic performance in pure prose rhythm.
Dickens tells us upfront: she has a good deal to say, chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation, but not much to tell.
"Why, Mrs. Piper has a good deal to say, chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation, but not much to tell."
That metafictional wink — Dickens describing his own punctuation choices as Mrs. Piper's speech mannerism — is the kind of structural joke that earns a very small and private smile.

But the formal enactment of the joke is what matters: Piper's speech actually is parenthetical, actually without punctuation — and it buries the one useful fact it contains about Jo beneath an avalanche of neighbourhood gossip.
The system produces this testimony. This is what testimony looks like when the voiceless cannot speak for themselves.
Reading Mrs. Piper aloud is one of the great athletic challenges in Dickens — you genuinely need breath control.
But underneath the comedy you feel the horror: this woman is being asked about a dead man and a homeless boy, and she is telling you about her infant Johnny's gum troubles.
The parenthetical style is not just funny — it is how indifference speaks when it is called to account.
And the one person who actually knows anything — the boy who sweeps the crossing, who has been seen speaking with the deceased — is there, noted, and never called.
That final image — the boy noted and never called — brings me to what I find most profound in this cluster of passages.
Dickens is not primarily a systems thinker. He is a moralist of the particular — of what one human being owes another.
And the novel's most surprising moral statement comes not from a reformer or an innocent child, but from Sir Leicester Dedlock in his ruin.
The narrator observes, of Leicester's grief and fidelity to his wife:

"Nothing less worthy can be seen through the lustre of such qualities in the commonest mechanic, nothing less worthy can be seen in the best-born gentleman. In such a light both aspire alike, both rise alike, both children of the dust shine equally."
'Children of the dust.' That phrase — extended to Jo and to Leicester, to the mechanic and the baronet alike — is Dickens's answer to every institution in the novel.
Not a programme. A vision of common humanity.
Edmund, that passage from the narrator moves me enormously — and I think it works structurally because the novel has earned it by then.
We have seen Tom at five years old walking up and down with a baby on his shoulder in a freezing room.
We have seen Jo's hands on the iron gate in the dark.
By the time Dickens writes 'children of the dust shine equally,' the reader has accumulated image after image of children who were never allowed to shine.
The philosophical statement has been built, brick by brick, out of observed suffering.
Children of the dust — it's a phrase that I think will stay with our listeners long after this conversation.

From the ferociously dissatisfied Pardiggle boys, to Tom nursing his sister in the cold, to Jo standing at the bars in the dark, to Leicester in his ruin — Dickens traces a single argument about who counts and who must be made to count.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Edmund Leigh, and Oliver Trevelyan.
We'll be back with our next segment of Bleak House Unpacked very shortly.

segments.title: Comic Relief and Coded Critique: Humor as Social Instrument

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've been tracing the novel's darker currents — but Dickens is also, let's not forget, one of the great comic writers in the language.
Today we're asking what his humor is actually doing — whether it's relief, or something sharper, more purposeful.
Eleanor Hartley is with us — she reads Dickens as an architect of effects, always asking how the machinery works.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings his conviction that great fiction is fundamentally about character and moral imagination.
And Oliver Trevelyan — who has read more Dickens aloud than perhaps anyone alive — hears rhythms and timing the rest of us can only guess at.
Oliver, I want to start with the Boodle passage — because those names alone are half the joke, aren't they?
They are, and they are also the whole point.
Listen to what Dickens does — Coodle, Doodle, Foodle, Goodle, Hoodle — the list just keeps rolling and the names get more preposterous with each addition.
And the bureaucratic precision of the distribution — the Home Department to Joodle, the Exchequer to Koodle — that mock-gravity is everything.
The sentence builds and builds, with complete apparent seriousness, and then it lands here — let me read it:
"What follows? That the country is shipwrecked, lost, and gone to pieces — as is made manifest to the patriotism of Sir Leicester Dedlock — because you can't provide for Noodle!"
The country is shipwrecked — because of Noodle.
That is a perfect comic sentence. Perfect in structure, perfect in timing, perfect in rage.
And what I love is that the rage is completely invisible on the surface.
Dickens doesn't editorialize. He simply performs the logic of the aristocratic political class with absolute fidelity — and lets that logic indict itself.
The narrator adds only that Sir Leicester finds this analysis a manifest demonstration of patriotism — which is the knife going in.
Structurally, it's what we'd call free indirect discourse taken to its satirical extreme.
Dickens inhabits the perspective so thoroughly that the critique needs no authorial intrusion whatsoever.
I won't quarrel with the technical description, but I'd push back gently on calling it critique in any programmatic sense.
What Dickens is really doing is something older and more English — he's writing in the tradition of the great comic satirists, of Fielding, of Swift.
The target is human vanity — the vanity of men who mistake the management of their own patronage networks for the governance of a nation.
That's a moral failing, not a systemic one. It's a comedy of character.
I think that's right — and yet it becomes something else when you hold it next to Jo.
Because Jo appears in the very next chapter, and the contrast is not accidental.
There's that extraordinary moment of testimony — this child, asked to give his name:
"No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school."
After Noodle, that lands like a blow.
The country that cannot find an office for Noodle cannot find a school for Jo.
That structural juxtaposition is, I think, the key to the whole novel's method.
Dickens doesn't argue his case — he arranges his material so that the reader's mind makes the connection involuntarily.
Look at how the Jo passage is written — that fragmentary syntax, those short declarative clauses.
"Knows a broom's a broom, and knows it's wicked to tell a lie."
That mimics a mind shaped only by the most immediate, concrete experience — a mind that has been given nothing else to work with.
The syntax itself is the argument.
The passage moves me — I won't pretend otherwise.
But what moves me is not the political implication. It is the boy himself — the character of Jo.
And what is most remarkable about Jo is what he remembers about the dead man — about Nemo.
The man turned back on a cold winter night and said — and this is the line I keep returning to:
"Neither have I. Not one!" and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging.
That is solidarity born of shared wretchedness — and it is a moral act, freely chosen.
Dickens, whatever his politics, understands that individual goodness is the thing that actually sustains human life.
And the boy carries that. He carries the weight of it at the inquest, wiping his eyes on that wretched sleeve.
You can't perform this passage without slowing down entirely. Dickens writes it for the voice:
"He wos wery good to me, he wos!"
The repetition — "he wos" — that's not an accident of dialect transcription.
That's a child reaching for emphasis with the only rhetorical tool he has — saying it again.
And it works. It works completely.
So the humor and the pathos aren't actually in opposition — they're part of the same instrument.
The Boodle passage makes you laugh at the absurdity of a governing class consumed by its own internal logistics.
And then Jo's testimony makes the cost of that absurdity devastating and specific.
Comic and tragic are not alternatives in Bleak House — they are two edges of the same blade.
Two edges of the same blade — that's a formulation worth sitting with.
A governing class too busy allocating offices for Noodle to notice Jo on his crossing.
In our next segment, we'll turn to how Dickens handles the institutions that were supposed to bridge that gap — and so comprehensively failed.

segments.title: Tangled Lives: How Dickens Weaves Individual Fates into Social Meaning

utterances.text: We come now to what I think is the emotional and architectural heart of Bleak House — the way Dickens braids individual lives into something larger.
Richard Carstone is the novel's great study in self-dissolution — a young man of genuine warmth who cannot hold himself together.
Eleanor, you've been circling Richard's arc all episode — I'd love to start with you on what Dickens is actually constructing here.
What Dickens is doing with Richard is almost cruelly precise as a piece of narrative engineering.
He doesn't give Richard a vice, exactly — he gives him an absence. An inability to cohere.
And the novel catches him naming that absence himself, which is the genius of it.
He says to Esther — and this is one of those moments where the character seems to have written himself —
"I seem to want something or other to stand by. Even you have no idea how fond I am of Ada — but I don't settle down to constancy in other things. It's such uphill work, and it takes such a time!"
That phrase — 'uphill work' — is so perfectly, devastatingly ordinary.
Constancy feels like a chore to him. Not a betrayal of values — just exhausting.
That is a diagnosis, not just a character note. And Dickens delivers it through Richard's own cheerful, self-exculpating voice.
Eleanor is right, and I'd press the point further. What Dickens understands — and this is profoundly Johnsonian — is that character is habit.
Richard is not destroyed by the Chancery suit — he is revealed by it. The weakness was always there.
Mrs. Badger — that magnificently comic figure — puts it with remarkable clarity when she tells Esther what Richard lacks.
"He has not that positive interest in it which makes it his vocation."
She contrasts him immediately with young Woodcourt, who takes his profession from genuine passion and will endure hardship for it.
The novel is full of such quiet structural contrasts — Dickens places characters in triangulation, not in isolation.
Richard is not simply weak — he is weak in a particular way that the world around him — Chancery above all — is perfectly designed to exploit.
That is what I call moral imagination. Not propaganda — tragedy.
I've read Richard aloud many times, and Edmund has it exactly — the tragedy is in the charm.
He's so likeable. You want to grab him by the collar and also — I confess — you simply enjoy being in his company.
And Esther catches that — she catches herself enjoying it.
When she describes Richard and Ada confiding in her — bringing their chairs either side of her — there is this gorgeous aside:
"They went on in their own wild way for a little while — I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself."
That semicolon is doing so much work. The slight confession tucked inside it — 'I enjoyed it too much myself.'
Esther is not some passive moral register. She is alive to the pleasure of these young people — even when she knows the danger.
For a performer, that is everything. The character who sees clearly and loves anyway — that is your heart of the novel.
Oliver's put his finger on something that matters enormously for how this novel is narrated.
Esther's narration is often read as prim — even unreliable in a slightly fusty, self-deprecating way.
But watch what she does in these scenes with Richard. She counsels him on duty — and she means it.
She tells him that his love for Ada carries a responsibility — that it was, as she phrases it,
"a part of his affectionate consideration for her not to slight the importance of a step that might influence both their lives."
That sentence is quietly devastating in its formality. She is not scolding him — she is appealing to his love as the ground of his duty.
And it works — briefly. He becomes 'almost grave.' Dickens can't even let him reach full gravity.
That adverb — 'almost' — contains his entire fate.
'Almost grave.' Eleanor has found the exact word and I shan't try to improve on it.
What I would add is that the scene with Ada and Esther in the earlier chapter is one of Dickens's finest passages of domestic tenderness.
The three of them sitting together half the night, talking — advising, as Esther says.
And the terms Esther lays down for young love are not cynical — they are precisely right.
That love could come to happiness only — she is precise about the word 'only' —
"if it were real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and perseverance, each always for the other's sake."
Constancy. Fortitude. Perseverance. Three words that form a complete moral architecture — and Richard will fail all three.
Dickens has planted the standard against which his collapse will be measured. That is craft of the highest order.
Edmund has described it as craft — and it is — but I'd call it something more like a long, slow heartbreak.
Because when you're reading this aloud — when you're Richard, in your voice — you can hear him meaning every word.
He absolutely intends to do what Esther asks. He loves Ada entirely. And still — he cannot hold.
Mrs. Badger's comparison to Woodcourt is pointed — Woodcourt's dedication comes from vocation, from deep in the bone.
She says those young men will find their reward, quote,
"through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
That is the path Richard cannot walk. Not from malice — from constitution.
And Dickens makes us love him in spite of it — which is far harder, and far sadder, than making us condemn him.
Richard Carstone — adored, well-intentioned, and constitutionally unable to become the man his love requires.
What this conversation has uncovered is that Dickens doesn't need villains to generate tragedy — he needs a world shaped perfectly to find its victims' weaknesses.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Sir Edmund Leigh, and Oliver Trevelyan for a conversation that has done justice to a great and inexhaustible novel.
Bleak House Unpacked will return. Until then — keep reading.

itself is made a dead letter. All through the deplorable cause,
everything that everybody in it, except one man, knows already is
referred to that only one man who don’t know, it to find out—all
through the deplorable cause, everybody must have copies, over and
over again, of everything that has accumulated about it in the way of
cartloads of papers (or must pay for them without having them, which
is the usual course, for nobody wants them) and must go down the
middle and up again through such an infernal country-dance of costs
and fees and nonsense and corruption as was never dreamed of in the
wildest visions of a witch’s Sabbath. Equity sends questions to law,
law sends questions back to equity; law finds it can’t do this,
equity finds it can’t do that; neither can so much as say it can’t do
anything, without this solicitor instructing and this counsel
appearing for A, and that solicitor instructing and that counsel
appearing for B; and so on through the whole alphabet, like the
history of the apple pie. And thus, through years and years, and
lives and lives, everything goes on, constantly beginning over and
over again, and nothing ever ends. And we can’t get out of the suit
on any terms, for we are made parties to it, and MUST BE parties to
it, whether we like it or not. But it won’t do to think of it! When
my great uncle, poor Tom Jarndyce, began to think of it, it was the
beginning of the end!”

meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers
of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city.

into the cabooses of collier-brigs; fog lying out on the yards and
hovering in the rigging of great ships; fog drooping on the gunwales
of barges and small boats. Fog in the eyes and throats of ancient
Greenwich pensioners, wheezing by the firesides of their wards; fog
in the stem and bowl of the afternoon pipe of the wrathful skipper,
down in his close cabin; fog cruelly pinching the toes and fingers of
his shivering little ’prentice boy on deck. Chance people on the
bridges peeping over the parapets into a nether sky of fog, with fog
all round them, as if they were up in a balloon and hanging in the
misty clouds.

another what you are to-day. All I say before speaking to you
according to that assumption is, if you DO change—if you DO come to
find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and
woman than you were as boy and girl (your manhood will excuse me,
Rick!)—don’t be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be
nothing monstrous or uncommon in it. I am only your friend and
distant kinsman. I have no power over you whatever. But I wish and
hope to retain your confidence if I do nothing to forfeit it.”
c13:p115.summary: Mr. Jarndyce counsels Ada and Richard that while he assumes their love will endure, if they change he will remain their confidant and will not judge them.

All I say before speaking to you according to that assumption is, if you DO change—if you DO come to find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and woman than you were as boy and girl (your manhood will excuse me, Rick!)—don't be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be nothing monstrous or uncommon in it.

c13:p118.text:
“Come!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “Now for our assumption. Now we lift our
eyes up and look hopefully at the distance! Rick, the world is before
you; and it is most probable that as you enter it, so it will receive
you. Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never
separate the two, like the heathen waggoner. Constancy in love is a
good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy
in every kind of effort. If you had the abilities of all the great
men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely
meaning it and setting about it. If you entertain the supposition
that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could
be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts,
leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here.”
c13:p118.summary: Mr. Jarndyce advises Richard to trust Providence and his own efforts equally, to combine constancy in love with diligent effort in all pursuits, and never to expect success without genuine commitment.

Constancy in love is a good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy in every kind of effort. c13:p124.text:
The door stood open, and we both followed them with our eyes as they
passed down the adjoining room, on which the sun was shining, and out
at its farther end. Richard with his head bent, and her hand drawn
through his arm, was talking to her very earnestly; and she looked up
in his face, listening, and seemed to see nothing else. So young, so
beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through
the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the
years to come and making them all years of brightness. So they passed
away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that
had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun
was clouded over.

c17:p75.text:
This was the first time I ever saw him follow Ada with his eyes with
something of a shadow on their benevolent expression. I well
remembered the look with which he had contemplated her and Richard
when she was singing in the firelight; it was but a very little while
since he had watched them passing down the room in which the sun was
shining, and away into the shade; but his glance was changed, and
even the silent look of confidence in me which now followed it once
more was not quite so hopeful and untroubled as it had originally
been.
c17:p75.summary: Esther observes for the first time that Mr. Jarndyce looks at Ada and Richard with a troubled shadow in his formerly benevolent gaze, suggesting hidden concern or emotion beyond that of a simple guardian.

c17:p62.text:
“If I went into Kenge’s office,” said Richard, “and if I were placed
under articles to Kenge, I should have my eye on the—hum!—the
forbidden ground—and should be able to study it, and master it, and
to satisfy myself that it was not neglected and was being properly
conducted. I should be able to look after Ada’s interests and my own
interests (the same thing!); and I should peg away at Blackstone and
all those fellows with the most tremendous ardour.”
c17:p62.summary: Richard explains that by entering Kenge's law office, he could monitor the Chancery suit while ostensibly studying law, revealing that his interest in law is entirely instrumental to his obsession with the suit.
c17:p62.best_quote: If I went into Kenge's office...I should have my eye on the—hum!—the forbidden ground—and should be able to study it, and master it

c23:p23.text:
At that time, and for a good many weeks after that time, Richard was
constant in his visits. Besides coming every Saturday or Sunday and
remaining with us until Monday morning, he sometimes rode out on
horseback unexpectedly and passed the evening with us and rode back
again early next day. He was as vivacious as ever and told us he was
very industrious, but I was not easy in my mind about him. It
appeared to me that his industry was all misdirected. I could not
find that it led to anything but the formation of delusive hopes in
connexion with the suit already the pernicious cause of so much
sorrow and ruin. He had got at the core of that mystery now, he told
us, and nothing could be plainer than that the will under which he
and Ada were to take I don’t know how many thousands of pounds must
be finally established if there were any sense or justice in the
Court of Chancery—but oh, what a great IF that sounded in my
ears—and that this happy conclusion could not be much longer
delayed. He proved this to himself by all the weary arguments on that
side he had read, and every one of them sunk him deeper in the
infatuation. He had even begun to haunt the court. He told us how he
saw Miss Flite there daily, how they talked together, and how he did
her little kindnesses, and how, while he laughed at her, he pitied
her from his heart. But he never thought—never, my poor, dear,
sanguine Richard, capable of so much happiness then, and with such
better things before him—what a fatal link was riveting between his
fresh youth and her faded age, between his free hopes and her caged
birds, and her hungry garret, and her wandering mind.
c23:p23.summary: Esther describes Richard's constant visits and his growing fixation on Chancery, his delusional belief in an imminent favorable judgment, his friendship with Miss Flite, and her ominous premonition of the catastrophic effect this will have on him.
c23:p23.best_quote: Every one of them sunk him deeper in the infatuation...what a fatal link was riveting between his fresh youth and her faded age, between his free hopes and her caged birds, and her hungry garret, and her wandering mind.

c17:p96.text:
“Nine years, my dear,” he said after thinking for a little while,
“have passed since I received a letter from a lady living in
seclusion, written with a stern passion and power that rendered it
unlike all other letters I have ever read. It was written to me (as
it told me in so many words), perhaps because it was the writer’s
idiosyncrasy to put that trust in me, perhaps because it was mine to
justify it. It told me of a child, an orphan girl then twelve years
old, in some such cruel words as those which live in your
remembrance. It told me that the writer had bred her in secrecy from
her birth, had blotted out all trace of her existence, and that if
the writer were to die before the child became a woman, she would be
left entirely friendless, nameless, and unknown. It asked me to
consider if I would, in that case, finish what the writer had begun.”
c17:p96.summary: Mr. Jarndyce recounts receiving a letter from a mysterious lady written with stern passion, asking him to provide for a twelve-year-old orphan girl described in harsh terms, requesting that he finish what the writer had begun.
c17:p96.best_quote: It was written to me (as it told me in so many words), perhaps because it was the writer's idiosyncrasy to put that trust in me, perhaps because it was mine to justify it. It told me of a child, an orphan girl then twelve years old, in some such cruel words as those which live in your remembrance.

c17:p98.text:
“Your early recollection, my dear, will supply the gloomy medium
through which all this was seen and expressed by the writer, and the
distorted religion which clouded her mind with impressions of the
need there was for the child to expiate an offence of which she was
quite innocent. I felt concerned for the little creature, in her
darkened life, and replied to the letter.”
c17:p98.summary: Mr. Jarndyce explains that the writer was driven by a distorted religious conviction that the innocent child must suffer expiation for an offense she did not commit, and that his compassion for this 'little creature' moved him to respond to her letter.
c17:p98.best_quote: the distorted religion which clouded her mind with impressions of the need there was for the child to expiate an offence of which she was quite innocent

c17:p100.text:
“It laid the injunction on me that I should never propose to see the
writer, who had long been estranged from all intercourse with the
world, but who would see a confidential agent if I would appoint one.
I accredited Mr. Kenge. The lady said, of her own accord and not of
his seeking, that her name was an assumed one. That she was, if there
were any ties of blood in such a case, the child’s aunt. That more
than this she would never (and he was well persuaded of the
steadfastness of her resolution) for any human consideration
disclose. My dear, I have told you all.”
c17:p100.summary: Mr. Jarndyce explains that the lady, who claims to be Esther's aunt, has maintained absolute secrecy about her identity and refused to provide any further information despite Mr. Kenge's mediation.
c17:p100.best_quote: That she was, if there were any ties of blood in such a case, the child's aunt. That more than this she would never (and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution) for any human consideration disclose.

c18:p42.text:
And, very strangely, there was something quickened within me,
associated with the lonely days at my godmother’s; yes, away even to
the days when I had stood on tiptoe to dress myself at my little
glass after dressing my doll. And this, although I had never seen
this lady’s face before in all my life—I was quite sure of
it—absolutely certain.
c18:p42.summary: Esther experiences a strange association between Lady Dedlock and her childhood memories, though she is certain they have never met.
c18:p42.best_quote: "And, very strangely, there was something quickened within me, associated with the lonely days at my godmother's; yes, away even to the days when I had stood on tiptoe to dress myself at my little glass after dressing my doll."

c18:p44.text:
I felt it to be an unmeaning weakness in me and tried to overcome it
by attending to the words I heard. Then, very strangely, I seemed to
hear them, not in the reader’s voice, but in the well-remembered
voice of my godmother. This made me think, did Lady Dedlock’s face
accidentally resemble my godmother’s? It might be that it did, a
little; but the expression was so different, and the stern decision
which had worn into my godmother’s face, like weather into rocks, was
so completely wanting in the face before me that it could not be that
resemblance which had struck me. Neither did I know the loftiness and
haughtiness of Lady Dedlock’s face, at all, in any one. And yet I—I,
little Esther Summerson, the child who lived a life apart and on
whose birthday there was no rejoicing—seemed to arise before my own
eyes, evoked out of the past by some power in this fashionable lady,
whom I not only entertained no fancy that I had ever seen, but whom I
perfectly well knew I had never seen until that hour.
c18:p44.summary: Esther analyzes her emotional response, considering but rejecting a resemblance to her godmother, while feeling her entire past self summoned by something in Lady Dedlock.
c18:p44.best_quote: "And yet I—I, little Esther Summerson, the child who lived a life apart and on whose birthday there was no rejoicing—seemed to arise before my own eyes, evoked out of the past by some power in this fashionable lady, whom I not only entertained no fancy that I had ever seen, but whom I perfectly well knew I had never seen until that hour."

c8:p55.text:
We had never seen such dissatisfied children. It was not merely that
they were weazened and shrivelled—though they were certainly that
too—but they looked absolutely ferocious with discontent. At the
mention of the Tockahoopo Indians, I could really have supposed
Egbert to be one of the most baleful members of that tribe, he gave
me such a savage frown. The face of each child, as the amount of his
contribution was mentioned, darkened in a peculiarly vindictive
manner, but his was by far the worst. I must except, however, the
little recruit into the Infant Bonds of Joy, who was stolidly and
evenly miserable.
c8:p55.summary: Esther observes that Mrs. Pardiggle's five sons are miserable, shriveled, and scowling, each darkening in malice as their meager contributions are mentioned.

I applied the key on hearing this and opened the door. In a poor room
with a sloping ceiling and containing very little furniture was a
mite of a boy, some five or six years old, nursing and hushing a
heavy child of eighteen months. There was no fire, though the weather
was cold; both children were wrapped in some poor shawls and tippets

c11:p98.text:
With the night comes a slouching figure through the tunnel-court to
the outside of the iron gate. It holds the gate with its hands and

c11:p74.text:

such was the sufferings gentlemen of that child in his gums) as the

which that report originatinin. See the plaintive often and
considered as his air was feariocious and not to be allowed to go

may be brought forard for she is here and will do credit to her

c58:p70.text:
His formal array of words might have at any other time, as it has
often had, something ludicrous in it, but at this time it is serious
and affecting. His noble earnestness, his fidelity, his gallant
shielding of her, his generous conquest of his own wrong and his own
pride for her sake, are simply honourable, manly, and true. Nothing
less worthy can be seen through the lustre of such qualities in the
commonest mechanic, nothing less worthy can be seen in the best-born
gentleman. In such a light both aspire alike, both rise alike, both
children of the dust shine equally.
c58:p70.summary: The narrator reflects that Sir Leicester's earnestness, fidelity, and generous conquering of his own pride for Lady Dedlock's sake transcend class and honor all humanity.
c58:p70.best_quote: "In such a light both aspire alike, both rise alike, both children of the dust shine equally."

c12:p56.text:
Then there is my Lord Boodle, of considerable reputation with his
party, who has known what office is and who tells Sir Leicester
Dedlock with much gravity, after dinner, that he really does not see
to what the present age is tending. A debate is not what a debate
used to be; the House is not what the House used to be; even a
Cabinet is not what it formerly was. He perceives with astonishment
that supposing the present government to be overthrown, the limited
choice of the Crown, in the formation of a new ministry, would lie
between Lord Coodle and Sir Thomas Doodle—supposing it to be
impossible for the Duke of Foodle to act with Goodle, which may be
assumed to be the case in consequence of the breach arising out of
that affair with Hoodle. Then, giving the Home Department and the
leadership of the House of Commons to Joodle, the Exchequer to
Koodle, the Colonies to Loodle, and the Foreign Office to Moodle,
what are you to do with Noodle? You can’t offer him the Presidency of
the Council; that is reserved for Poodle. You can’t put him in the
Woods and Forests; that is hardly good enough for Quoodle. What
follows? That the country is shipwrecked, lost, and gone to pieces
(as is made manifest to the patriotism of Sir Leicester Dedlock)
because you can’t provide for Noodle!
c12:p56.summary: Lord Boodle explains to Sir Leicester that government is failing because there is no office suitable for Noodle after all the important positions are distributed among his equally mediocre associates.
c12:p56.best_quote: What follows? That the country is shipwrecked, lost, and gone to pieces (as is made manifest to the patriotism of Sir Leicester Dedlock) because you can't provide for Noodle!

c11:p78.text:
Name, Jo. Nothing else that he knows on. Don’t know that everybody
has two names. Never heerd of sich a think. Don’t know that Jo is
short for a longer name. Thinks it long enough for HIM. HE don’t find
no fault with it. Spell it? No. HE can’t spell it. No father, no
mother, no friends. Never been to school. What’s home? Knows a
broom’s a broom, and knows it’s wicked to tell a lie. Don’t recollect
who told him about the broom or about the lie, but knows both. Can’t
exactly say what’ll be done to him arter he’s dead if he tells a lie
to the gentlemen here, but believes it’ll be something wery bad to
punish him, and serve him right—and so he’ll tell the truth.
c11:p78.summary: Jo testifies to his name, complete social isolation, illiteracy, and basic moral beliefs despite having no formal education.
c11:p78.best_quote: No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school.

c11:p87.text:
That graceless creature only knows that the dead man (whom he
recognized just now by his yellow face and black hair) was sometimes
hooted and pursued about the streets. That one cold winter night when
he, the boy, was shivering in a doorway near his crossing, the man
turned to look at him, and came back, and having questioned him and
found that he had not a friend in the world, said, “Neither have I.
Not one!” and gave him the price of a supper and a night’s lodging.
That the man had often spoken to him since and asked him whether he
slept sound at night, and how he bore cold and hunger, and whether he
ever wished to die, and similar strange questions. That when the man
had no money, he would say in passing, “I am as poor as you to-day,
Jo,” but that when he had any, he had always (as the boy most
heartily believes) been glad to give him some.
c11:p87.summary: Jo reveals the dead man recognized him, showed him kindness, asked about his welfare, and when poor himself, shared what little he had.
c11:p87.best_quote: Neither have I. Not one! and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging.

c11:p88.text:
“He was wery good to me,” says the boy, wiping his eyes with his
wretched sleeve. “Wen I see him a-layin’ so stritched out just now, I
wished he could have heerd me tell him so. He wos wery good to me, he
wos!”
c11:p88.summary: Jo weeps while expressing his gratitude and affection for the dead man.
c11:p88.best_quote: He wos wery good to me, he wos!

c17:p52.text:
“My dear Mother Hubbard,” he said, “that’s the very thing! I have
thought of that several times and have been quite angry with myself
for meaning to be so much in earnest and—somehow—not exactly being
so. I don’t know how it is; I seem to want something or other to
stand by. Even you have no idea how fond I am of Ada (my darling
cousin, I love you, so much!), but I don’t settle down to constancy
in other things. It’s such uphill work, and it takes such a time!”
said Richard with an air of vexation.
